1) Answer

Short answer: There is evidence that Nigel Farage consistently prioritises some core civil liberties (especially privacy from the state and freedom of speech), but his record also shows opposition to universal, treaty‑based human-rights protections (for example, the ECHR). So if “values human rights” means valuing civil liberties for citizens within a sovereign, UK‑only framework, you can point to credible evidence. If it means upholding universal, treaty‑based human rights that apply to everyone, the evidence is mixed.

Evidence that he values key civil liberties:
- Privacy/civil liberties against state overreach: Farage has opposed government ID schemes on civil‑liberties grounds, arguing they expand state power over ordinary people. In September 2025 he criticised proposed digital ID cards as expanding state control; in earlier remarks he even cited personal privacy concerns about being “tracked” via Oyster cards. These positions align with a pro‑privacy, anti‑surveillance view of individual rights. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2025/sep/27/petition-opposing-starmer-plan-digital-id-cards?utm_source=openai))
- Free speech as a foundational right: In 2025 testimony to the U.S. Congress, Farage argued the UK’s Online Safety Act and similar rules threaten free expression and repeatedly framed robust free speech as a bedrock liberty (“you can say what you like… because that’s what free speech is”), invoking the UK’s constitutional tradition to justify his stance. This is a clear, repeated defense of a classic human right. ([time.com](https://time.com/7314225/nigel-farage-congress-hearing-trump-relationship-free-speech/?utm_source=openai))
- Preference for a domestic Bill of Rights to protect liberties: Farage’s platform has argued for replacing the Human Rights Act with a UK Bill of Rights, described by allies as focusing on individual liberties such as free speech and due process under domestic law. While critics dispute the details, the stated aim is to protect rights via UK institutions rather than Strasbourg. ([independent.co.uk](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/nigel-farage-keir-starmer-reform-uk-angela-eagle-reform-b2813814.html?utm_source=openai))

Important limitations and counter‑evidence:
- Treaties and universality: Farage has championed leaving the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and repealing the Human Rights Act to enable mass deportations and curb asylum rights, positions many legal experts and officials say would undercut universal rights protections and potentially affect the Good Friday Agreement. He and Reform UK have said a replacement Bill of Rights would primarily cover British citizens and those lawfully resident, narrowing the traditional universality of human rights. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/uks-farage-unveils-plan-deport-asylum-seekers-warns-civil-disorder-2025-08-26/?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: You can credibly “prove” that Farage values certain human rights—especially free speech and privacy from excessive state power—within a UK‑sovereign framework. But his proposals to quit the ECHR and limit protections for non‑citizens mean the claim is not proven if “human rights” is taken in the universal, treaty‑based sense.
